title: p0162
universal_lens: The universal lens formalizes temporal discounting as a hyperbolic decay operator acting on competing action potentials. The dominance of an action is strictly governed by the coarse ratio of its delay relative to alternatives, establishing a foundational metric for evaluating time-discounted value across disparate physical and cognitive systems.
gsi_mapping: In GSI, this primitive maps to Bayesian inference over delayed reward signals. A coarser delay ratio between two betting outcomes yields a steeper posterior gradient, requiring fewer empirical observations (training trials) to achieve a specified confidence threshold in selecting the shorter-delay outcome.
gse_mapping: For GSE situational reasoning, this defines a state-transition kernel where agents optimize path selection under latency constraints. The transition probability toward a goal with lesser delay accelerates non-linearly as the delay differential widens, dictating optimal routing in dynamic, multi-agent environments.

primitives.name: Delay Ratio Dominance Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Other things equal, the coarser the ratio of the delay of reinforcement of two competing reactions, the less will be the training required to give the act involving the lesser delay a given degree of dominance.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Ratio of delays: dimensionless; Training trials: integer count; Dominance: probability (0 to 1)
primitives.assumptions: All other environmental variables and baseline reinforcement magnitudes remain constant; the system exhibits standard hyperbolic temporal discounting properties.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Fails when the absolute delay exceeds the agent's maximum memory horizon or when immediate survival imperatives override long-term optimization.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to the Kullback-Leibler divergence rate between two exponentially decaying reward distributions. A larger delay ratio increases the distinguishability of the distributions, accelerating convergence.
layer2.telemetry: Number of reinforcements/trials required to reach a fixed dominance threshold (e.g., 80% choice frequency).

primitives.name: Empirical Convergence Acceleration Metric
primitives.verbatim_quote: The 30-90-second discrimination reached, between 15 and 20 reinforcements, a degree of short-delay dominance only attained by the 30-60-second combination between the 35th and 40th reinforcements.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Time delays: seconds (s); Reinforcements: discrete event count; Dominance degree: normalized probability
primitives.assumptions: Learning curves follow a smooth, monotonic progression without catastrophic forgetting or sudden environmental shifts during the trial blocks.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down if the delay ratio approaches unity (1:1), causing the learning curves to asymptotically merge and rendering discrimination statistically impossible within finite trials.

layer2.mapping: Maps directly to the GSE state-update velocity. The derivative of the dominance function with respect to trial count is inversely proportional to the logarithmic delay ratio.
layer2.telemetry: Delta in trial counts ($\Delta N$) required to achieve identical dominance levels across varying delay ratios.

reasoning_traces.think:
The derivation begins by modeling the subjective value $V$ of a reinforcement as a function of its delay $\tau$, typically following a hyperbolic form $V(\tau) = A / (1 + k\tau)$. When two competing reactions are presented with delays $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$, the dominance of the shorter delay is determined by the ratio of their discounted values. The 'coarseness' of the delay ratio $r = \tau_2 / \tau_1$ dictates the initial separation of these value functions. Mathematically, a larger $r$ implies a greater instantaneous gradient in the value difference, which translates to a faster rate of information accumulation during training. This is empirically verified by Anderson's data, where a 1:3 ratio achieves target dominance significantly faster than a 1:2 ratio. The dualities emerge between the temporal domain (delays) and the statistical domain (sample complexity). The failure mode occurs when the delays are too similar, causing the signal-to-noise ratio of the preference to drop below the detection threshold of the learning algorithm, leading to prolonged indecision or random exploration.
